title: Raise Your Sum Insured or Buy Riders? How Experts Say to Prioritise
excerpt: A cheap super top-up can take family cover to Rs 1 crore for about Rs 4,500 a year - but riders like consumables cover and critical-illness protection still earn their place. Here is how to prioritise.
body:
• A super top-up is usually the cheapest way to raise cover: a ₹10 lakh super top-up for a family of four costs roughly ₹4,500 a year, versus ₹10,000–12,000 to add the same ₹10 lakh to a base plan — and the ideal target is about ₹1 crore of total cover.
  • Super top-ups aggregate all claims in a policy year against the deductible, while top-ups pay only when a single claim crosses it — the former suits multiple smaller hospitalisations.
  • Riders still earn their place for specific gaps: consumables cover (8–13% of a hospital bill), critical-illness lump sums, OPD and no-claim-bonus protection — but a standalone critical-illness plan beats a rider.

As hospital bills climb and medical inflation in India runs at 11.5–14% a year, most families with a ₹5 lakh health policy are underinsured — and the question comes up every renewal season: spend on riders, or just raise the sum insured? The expert consensus, drawn from Mint's reporting and industry guidance, points to a clear hierarchy. It starts not with either option, but with a third: the super top-up.

The super top-up first

A super top-up is dramatically cheaper than raising a base plan because of the deductible — it pays only after your cumulative claims in a policy year cross a threshold. Mint's guidance: keep a ₹10 lakh base policy and add a ₹90 lakh super top-up to reach roughly ₹1 crore of total cover. The numbers make the case: a ₹10 lakh super top-up for a family of four (two adults, two children, around 35) costs only about ₹4,500 a year, versus ₹10,000–12,000 a year to raise a base plan by the same ₹10 lakh.

Super top-ups work best with a base cover of at least ₹5–10 lakh, since they kick in only when the base sum insured is exhausted. And the mechanical distinction matters: a top-up pays only when a single claim crosses the deductible, while a super top-up aggregates all claims in the policy year and pays once total expenses cross it — so it allows multiple claims in a year.

Where riders earn their place

Once the cover ceiling is fixed, riders fill specific gaps the base policy leaves. The most defensible ones: consumables cover — gloves, syringes, PPE kits and attendant charges typically excluded from base policies, amounting to 8–13% of a hospital bill and up to ₹2–3 lakh for extended stays; critical illness, which pays a lump sum on diagnosis for income replacement during recovery; OPD cover; no-claim-bonus protection; and personal accident.

"It is better to buy a standalone critical illness plan than a rider. Standalone plans are far more comprehensive — they cover more diseases, many of which do not require hospitalisation."

— Kapil Mehta, co-founder, SecureNow Insurance Broker, speaking to Mint

On critical illness specifically, experts draw a line: if you already hold a comprehensive plan with a high sum insured, a critical-illness rider may be unnecessary — and where you do want the protection, a standalone critical-illness plan is preferable to a rider, covering more diseases with higher, more relevant sums assured.

The case for caution

Riders are not free money. One documented case study found riders arriving with 18–24-month waiting periods, narrow exclusions and roughly ₹24,600 a year in premium creep — the policyholder cancelled them and redirected the premiums into a liquid fund for first-line medical liquidity. It is a single anecdote, not expert consensus, but it captures the right instinct: audit what each rider actually covers before renewing it.

Premiums quoted here are indicative and insurer-specific; the ₹4,500 super top-up figure is an example, not a universal price. Read the deductible, the waiting periods and the exclusions — the cheap cover is only cheap if it pays when you need it.

A note for the diaspora

This is a live question for NRIs insuring parents back in India: a ₹5 lakh base policy bought years ago is being outgrown by costs, and a super top-up is the cheapest way to bring aging parents' cover up to a realistic level without re-underwriting a new base plan at older ages. Light-touch, but worth doing before the next renewal.
